overview:
Anashana (Skt. *anāśana*, Prakrit *anāsaṇa*) is a classical Jain term referring to deliberate reduction or cessation of food intake as a disciplined austerity (*tapas*). In the canonical and commentarial traditions, it is classified as one of the external austerities (*bāhya tapa*), specifically the practice of fasting with carefully defined intentions, boundaries, and ethical safeguards. Unlike casual or health‑related fasting, anashana is framed within the Jain soteriological project: reducing passions, cultivating equanimity, and weakening karmic influx (*āsrava*). It is not a stand‑alone practice but part of a structured ethical and meditative regimen for householders and monastics.

Across Jain traditions, anashana is distinguished from extreme or harmful deprivation. Primary texts repeatedly emphasize that fasting must be voluntary, non-coercive, and undertaken only when physical and mental conditions permit. For laypeople, anashana appears in graded forms—such as *upavāsa*, *ekāṣaṇa*, and *bhojana‑parimāṇa*—each with specific rules regarding timing, intention, and permissible exceptions. Monastic codes describe additional forms, but always with supervision, self-assessment, and the requirement that the practitioner remain capable of fulfilling ethical duties.

Anashana is also conceptually distinct from *sallekhanā*, the final vow. While both involve food reduction, anashana is a temporary austerity aimed at purification, whereas sallekhanā is a terminal vow requiring strict conditions, community oversight, and explicit prohibitions against self-harm. Classical sources treat them separately and warn against conflating them. In modern scholarship, anashana is studied within the broader Jain ascetic system, highlighting its ritual, ethical, and psychological dimensions.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.3
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.notes: This sutra classifies anashana as one of the six external austerities (*bāhya tapa*). Commentaries (e.g., Pūjyapāda’s *Sarvārthasiddhi*) explain that anashana includes full fasting, partial fasting, and regulated eating, all undertaken with equanimity.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 30.6
primary_sources.author: Attributed to early Śvetāmbara canonical redactors
primary_sources.translation: “Fasting is an austerity, and discipline must be practiced skillfully.”
primary_sources.notes: This passage situates fasting within a broader framework of disciplined conduct. The chapter emphasizes mindfulness, non-violence, and self-restraint as prerequisites for any austerity.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga Sūtra 1.7
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.original_text: जोगं समणो करेज्जा, अणासणं च धारेज्जा।
primary_sources.transliteration: jogaṃ samaṇo karejjā, aṇāsaṇaṃ ca dhārejjā
primary_sources.translation: “A monk should practice discipline and uphold fasting.”
primary_sources.notes: The text describes fasting as part of monastic discipline but repeatedly warns against harming oneself or neglecting essential duties. Commentaries stress that fasting must be proportionate to one’s capacity.

primary_sources.title: Mūlācāra 5.89 (Digambara)
primary_sources.author: Vattakera
primary_sources.translation: “Fasting is an austerity, provided it does not injure the body.”
primary_sources.notes: A key Digambara monastic code explicitly states that fasting must not violate non-harm (*ahiṃsā*) toward one’s own body. This is one of the clearest canonical safeguards against harmful deprivation.

misconceptions.myth: Anashana is the same as sallekhanā (the final vow).
misconceptions.reality: Anashana is a temporary austerity for purification; sallekhanā is a terminal vow with strict ethical and procedural requirements. Primary texts treat them as distinct practices with different aims.

misconceptions.myth: Jain fasting encourages extreme or harmful deprivation.
misconceptions.reality: Canonical sources repeatedly warn against self-harm and require that fasting be voluntary, moderate, and appropriate to one’s physical condition. Digambara and Śvetāmbara codes explicitly prohibit harmful fasting.
Laypeople also practice anashana in graded forms such as upavāsa and ekāṣaṇa. Household practice is carefully regulated and adapted to daily responsibilities.

misconceptions.myth: Anashana is primarily a ritual for merit.
misconceptions.reality: While merit (*puṇya*) may be associated with disciplined fasting, primary texts emphasize its role in reducing passions, cultivating equanimity, and limiting karmic influx.
